elements.reason: The abstract does not contain any statement identifying the report as a systematic review; sections are labeled Objective, Data Sources, Study Selection, Data Extraction, Data Synthesis, and Conclusions without explicitly labeling the work as a systematic review or meta-analysis.

elements.quote: Objective: To compare the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms in people after stroke.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states the review objective/question.

elements.quote: Study Selection: We included randomized controlled trials comparing non-pharmacological interventions to control conditions for depressive symptoms in people following stroke.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main inclusion criteria regarding design, intervention, comparator, outcome, and population.

elements.quote: Data Sources: A literature search was performed through the following databases from January 2000 to August 2018: MEDLINE; CINAHL Plus; Scopus; Academic Search Complete; Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials; Scopus; and Library, Information Science and Technology Abstracts.
elements.reason: The abstract names the information sources and the search period (through August 2018).

elements.quote: All trials were included once their outcome assessments were blinded.
elements.reason: The abstract hints at a quality/blinding-based assessment but does not explicitly specify a risk of bias assessment method.

elements.quote: Data Synthesis: Thirteen non-pharmacological interventions were categorized into four types... Overall beneficial effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms were found both post-intervention (effect size [ES] = -0.24, 95% confidence Interval [CI]: -0.37 to -0.11, p < 0.05)
elements.reason: The abstract describes the synthesis methods, including categorization of interventions and meta-analytic effect size estimation.

elements.quote: Of 1703 identified articles, 22 trials were included in narrative synthesis, of which 13 were eligible for meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (22 trials) and participant numbers per intervention type for the meta-analysis, but not the total number of participants across all included trials.

elements.quote: Overall beneficial effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms were found both post-intervention (effect size [ES] = -0.24, 95% confidence Interval [CI]: -0.37 to -0.11, p < 0.05) and at follow-up (ES = -0.22, CI: -0.36 to -0.07, p < 0.05). We found individual beneficial effects for complementary and alternative therapy (ES = -0.29, CI: -0.55 to -0.02, p < 0.05) and psychosocial therapy (ES = - 0.33, CI: -0.60 to -0.06, p < 0.05) post-intervention.
elements.reason: The abstract reports results for the main outcome (depressive symptoms), with numbers of trials and participants per intervention type provided in the Data Synthesis section.

elements.quote: Overall beneficial effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms were found both post-intervention (effect size [ES] = -0.24, 95% confidence Interval [CI]: -0.37 to -0.11, p < 0.05) and at follow-up (ES = -0.22, CI: -0.36 to -0.07, p < 0.05).
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports summary effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals.

elements.quote: Overall beneficial effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms were found both post-intervention... We found individual beneficial effects for complementary and alternative therapy... and psychosocial therapy
elements.reason: The abstract indicates the direction of effect, stating that effects were beneficial for non-pharmacological interventions versus control conditions, and identifies which intervention types were favored.
The abstract's Conclusions section does not summarize limitations of the included evidence such as risk of bias, inconsistency, or imprecision.

elements.quote: Conclusions: Non-pharmacological interventions can be effective in addressing depressive symptoms in people after stroke. Complementary and alternative therapy and psychosocial therapy appear to be promising strategies for improving post-stroke depressive symptoms. Future studies are required to identify a personalized approach for people with specific conditions such as cognitive impairment.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an interpretation of the results and their implications for practice and future research.
The abstract does not state the funding source for the review.
The abstract does not report a registration name or registration number.

elements.quote: Three meta-analyses have been conducted to provide synthesized evidence on the effectiveness of pharmacological interventions for depressive symptoms following stroke, but results were mixed... With mixed conclusions, the effectiveness of pharmacological interventions for post-stroke depressive symptoms has not yet been determined.
elements.reason: The introduction describes current knowledge, including mixed results of pharmacological meta-analyses and existing qualitative NPI reviews, identifying the uncertainty.

elements.quote: For these reasons, an alternative, or addition, to pharmaceutical options is essential to ensure effective management of depressive symptoms after stroke... Therefore, to address this research gap, this study aimed to conduct a meta-analysis to synthesize and compare the available evidence regarding the effectiveness of various NPIs for treating depression in people following stroke.
elements.reason: The need and importance of the review are explicitly explained, citing unaddressed depression consequences, limitations of pharmacological options, and the research gap.

elements.quote: Three reviews have identified several NPIs for post-stroke depression and have qualitatively provided evidence. 8,11,14 However, none of these reviews quantitatively demonstrated the effectiveness of different types of NPIs.
elements.reason: Existing similar reviews are identified and cited, and the need for the current quantitative review is explained.

elements.quote: NPIs, which are defined as science-based and non-invasive interventions on human health, may provide an alternative to ameliorate depressive symptoms. Several NPIs for depression exist, such as complementary and alternative therapy (CAT), exercise, psychosocial therapy, non-invasive cranial stimulation, and multifactorial behavioral treatment.
elements.reason: The rationale for NPIs as an alternative is given and intervention types are listed, but no explicit mechanism of action for the interventions is described.
No logic model or description of hypothesized relationships between intervention components and outcomes is reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Objective: To compare the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms in people after stroke.
elements.reason: The review objective is explicitly stated in the abstract's Objective line, clearly expressing the review question.

elements.quote: The PICOS (Participants, Interventions, Comparisons, Outcomes, Study Designs) checklist was used to identify the inclusion criteria in this review.
elements.reason: The planned comparisons are defined using the PICOS framework, explicitly specifying participants, interventions, comparisons (NPIs vs control conditions such as usual treatment), outcomes, and study designs.

elements.quote: The PICOS (Participants, Interventions, Comparisons, Outcomes, Study Designs) checklist was used to identify the inclusion criteria in this review... This review considered any RCT with a pre-post design, meaning that outcomes were measured at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and follow-up.
elements.reason: Full PICOS-based eligibility criteria are specified, including participants (stroke, excluding manic/psychotic episodes), interventions/controls, outcomes (validated depression scale), and study design (RCTs with pre-post design and follow-up).

elements.reason: Report characteristics are specified: English language, peer-reviewed publication status; publication year range (January 2000–August 2018) is given in text_5.

The review does not distinguish exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported; exclusions are described only via inclusion criteria and JBI quality appraisal.

elements.quote: We computed standardized mean differences (SMDs) based on between-group comparisons of pre-post (or follow-up) change in scores and pre-test SDs.

elements.quote: We computed standardized mean differences (SMDs) based on between-group comparisons of pre-post (or follow-up) change in scores and pre-test SDs... If the study reported the pre- and post-test means in each group, we obtained the changes by subtracting the post-test outcome from the pre-test outcome within each group. Where the pre-test SD was not available, we used the change in SDs. In cases in which the study only reported standard errors (SEs), the SD was calculated using the following formula: SD = SE × number of participants.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes data preparation methods: computing change scores from pre/post means, handling missing pre-test SDs, converting SEs to SDs, and calculating SMDs for synthesis.

elements.quote: Appendix D.: Funnel plots: (a) a funnel plot including all included trials; (b) a funnel plot excluding three trials that showed publication bias on plot (a)

elements.quote: We visually inspected the potential of publication bias by a funnel plot, examining asymmetry of the graph.
elements.reason: The Methods describe use of a funnel plot for publication bias, and RevMan output (forest plots, Figure 2) is implied, but graphical display methods such as forest plots are not explicitly described in the Methods.
No basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs (e.g., by intervention type, chronology) is reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Funnel plots: (a) a funnel plot including all included trials; (b) a funnel plot excluding three trials that showed publication bias on plot (a)

elements.quote: For the meta-analysis, we calculated effect sizes and statistical heterogeneity using Review Manager (RevMan) 5.3 software (Nordic Cochrane Centre, Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen 2014).
elements.reason: Software package and version (RevMan 5.3) are explicitly reported.

elements.quote: We applied the random effect model in all calculations of effect size because all included trials had variations in study design, intervention methods, and population characteristics.
elements.reason: Random-effects model used with explicit rationale reported.

elements.quote: To obtain effect sizes, SMDs and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using Cohen's d test in which the pooled effect estimate (ie, depressive symptoms) was assessed using various measurements.
